header: For Appellant Mr. Munsif Saeed, Advocate
For Respondents Mr. Muhammad Arif, Advocate
J U D G M E N T
body: *** BABAR SATTAR, J. The appellant has impugned the judgment and decree dated 25.11.2024, whereby the suit filed by the respondents under Section 3 of the Defamation Ordinance, 2002 (“Defamation Ordinance”), was decreed and the appellant was directed to pay compensatory damages of Rs. 0.5 million to the respondents jointly.

2. The respondents filed a suit for defamation and recovery of damages amounting to Rs. 90 million under Section 3 of the Defamation Ordinance. They pleaded that they were well-reputed professionals and individuals enjoying standing in society, but had been defamed by false complaints filed by the appellant before the DPO and DC, Swabi. In those complaints, the appellant alleged that the respondents were part of the Qabza Mafia and had encroached upon and desecrated a graveyard containing the ancestral graves of the appellant’s predecessors. The respondents contended that the complaints were found to be false and were accordingly filed. However, the complaints had been circulated in the offices of the DPO and DC, prompting the initiation of inquiry proceedings to investigate the allegations that the respondents were part of the Qabza Mafia and had encroached upon a graveyard. It was further contended that the allegations had lowered the respondents in the estimation of right-thinking members of society and injured their reputations, for which they claimed damages amounting to Rs. 90 million.

3. The appellant filed a written statement, acknowledging the filing and contents of the complaints and reiterating the allegations contained therein. He maintained that the respondents had been interfering with a graveyard in Doaba Khel for a long time, were not well-reputed persons in the locality, and were involved in various illegal activities.
4. In view of the plaint and the written statement, the District Court framed the following issues:

1. Whether the plaintiffs have a cause of action? OPP 2. Whether suit of plaintiffs is within time? OPP 3. Whether the suit is not competent in its present form? OPD 4. Whether suit of the plaintiffs is not covered by the ambit and definition of Defamation Ordinance, 2002? OPD 5. Whether the defendant has filed false, libelous and defamatory complaints against the plaintiffs, if so its effects? OPP 6. Whether due to false, libellous and defamatory complaints lodged by the defendant against the plaintiffs, they have suffered an incalculable physical and mental harm? OPP 7. Whether due to unwarranted and irresponsible act of the defendant, plaintiffs are entitled to be compensated, if so, to what extent? OPP 8. Relief.

5. Issues Nos. 1 to 4 were decided by the District Court in favour of the respondents. The District Court held that the term “Qabza Mafia” was derogatory and defamatory and that such an allegation had been levelled against the respondents without being proved true. The defamatory statements had been communicated to the police and local administration and constituted libel. The respondents, therefore, had a cause of action to sue the appellant. The defamation suit was preceded by a legal notice issued by the respondents to the appellant and was filed within the prescribed limitation period of two months. The suit was held to be competent. In relation to Issues Nos. 5 and 6, the District Court held that the appellant had admitted filing a complaint describing the respondents as part of a “Qabza Group”. After filing the first complaint, the appellant repeated the allegations by filing another complaint with the local administration. Both complaints were found to be without merit. The allegations against the respondents were defamatory and had harmed their reputations, in which case the infliction of injury was presumed.

6. The District Court noted that the respondents had led evidence through Muhammad Nawaz Khan (PW-5), whose testimony was consistent and remained unshaken during cross-examination, reaffirming the contents of the plaint. The District Court also noted that the appellant had testified that he was working as a stenographer in the District Court, Swabi, from which it was evident that he was familiar with legal principles. Upon appraisal of the evidence, the District Court concluded that the appellant had failed to justify the accusations made against the respondents. Although he reiterated the allegations in his testimony, he produced no material to substantiate them. He relied upon certain FIRs, which did not establish illegal conduct on the part of the respondents, particularly when they had been acquitted in those cases. The District Court further noted that the appellant was unable to rely upon any of the defences listed in Section 5 of the Defamation Ordinance. It concluded that publication of the defamatory statements by the appellant had been established and that the statements were assertions rather than fair opinion. The allegations had been found false by the police authorities and the district administration. The statements were not protected by absolute or qualified privilege, and their reiteration by the appellant demonstrated recklessness on his part. The allegations portraying the respondents as dishonest individuals involved in criminal conduct, as members of the Qabza Mafia, and as persons seeking to desecrate a graveyard would naturally lower them in the estimation of society and harm their reputations. The District Court accordingly awarded general damages of Rs. 0.5 million, payable by the appellant to the respondents, keeping in view the appellant’s financial condition and the fact that the allegations had not been widely published or circulated.

7. Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that there was no cause of action for filing the suit for damages, as the appellant had made complaints in public interest to the authorities. He argued that filing a complaint with public authorities did not constitute publication within the meaning of Section 2(e) of the Defamation Ordinance. He further submitted that the appellant’s acts did not constitute defamation within the meaning of Section 3 of the Defamation Ordinance. He contended that, under Section 4 of the Defamation Ordinance, defamation was an actionable wrong only if it was proved. That the respondents were required to prove that the allegations were false but had failed to discharge such burden. He submitted that there was a distinction between allegations that had not been proved and allegations that had been found to be false. The mere filing of complaints with the police authorities and district administration could not, in itself, establish the falsity of the allegations. He further argued that the respondents had failed to establish how any damage had been caused to them and that, in the absence of such proof, damages could not be awarded.

8. Learned counsel for the respondents submitted that the communication of defamatory words to a person other than the person defamed constituted publication for the purposes of Section 2(e) of the Defamation Ordinance, and that this requirement had been satisfied in the instant case. He argued that the constituent elements of defamation under Section 3 of the Defamation Ordinance had been established, as the allegations made by the appellant had been found false by the police authorities and the district administration, both of which had conducted inquiries. The appellant had also failed to establish the truth of the allegations before the District Court. The written allegations constituted libel and lowered the respondents in the estimation of right-thinking members of society, as had correctly been held by the District Court. The appellant had admitted describing the respondents as part of the Qabza Mafia. Learned counsel submitted that the respondents were honourable individuals who had been involved in professional, social and political activities and belonged to a family of Maliks/Lambardars. The appellant had also failed to establish that the respondents had ever been convicted of an offence or that any illegality had been established against them. It had rightly been held that the mere registration of an FIR was no basis for classifying an individual as a criminal or as part of the Qabza Mafia. The allegations were assertions that were false and did not amount to fair and balanced opinion on the appellant’s part. The malicious nature of the allegations was evident from the fact that they had been levelled not against one individual but against the members of an entire family, thereby demonstrating malice and recklessness on the part of the appellant. Learned counsel submitted that the District Court had already taken a lenient view in awarding general damages and that there was no reason to interfere with the impugned judgment.

9. The appellant filed a complaint with the DPO, Swabi, alleging that the respondents were part of the Qabza Mafia and intended to desecrate and encroach upon the appellant’s ancestral graveyard. It was further alleged that the respondents had previously been held liable for encroachment and had engaged in illegal activities. The complaint was investigated by the police authorities through an inquiry and, having been found without merit, was filed. The appellant subsequently filed a second complaint with the district administration, which was also found to be without merit and was filed. Thereafter, the respondents served a legal notice upon the appellant. The first notice was returned because the appellant had left the address mentioned therein. The respondents then sent another notice to a different address, stated to be the appellant’s current address, but he refused to accept it. The respondents produced the relevant witnesses from the post office, along with the notices, to establish compliance with the condition precedent for filing a defamation suit.

10. The respondents produced the record keeper from the office of the Deputy Commissioner as PW-1, who produced the complaint and the relevant record showing its filing. They also produced the record keeper from the office of the Deputy Commissioner as PW-2, who produced the original complaint and the relevant record. The witnesses confirmed service of the legal notice upon the appellant appeared as PW-3 and PW-4. Muhammad Nawaz Khan, plaintiff No. 5, appeared as PW-5 and was subjected to cross-examination. He reiterated the contents of the plaint and stated that neither he nor any of the other respondents had ever been found liable for criminal conduct. He testified about the credentials and antecedents of the respondents and provided details of various legal proceedings, including the acquisition of certain property owned by the respondents, for which they had been compensated. The respondents also produced Mr. Ali Bahadar, a co-villager, as PW-6. He testified about the family’s antecedents and stated that its members were well regarded in the locality.

11. The appellant, on the other hand, appeared as a witness and reiterated the allegations contained in the complaints. He alleged that the respondents had erected a wall on the western side of the graveyard in question but produced no proof of that allegation. He produced various FIRs in which some of the respondents had been named and further alleged that the respondents had constructed a shop in the thoroughfare behind their Hujra. He also testified that Muhammad Nawaz Khan had received only a small number of votes in an election for Tehsil Nazim. His testimony reiterated the allegations levelled against the respondents in the complaints filed by him. He acknowledged that he had not filed any civil suit against the respondents. He was also unable to produce any evidence of a declaration by a court of law or any other public authority establishing that the respondents were liable for illegal conduct. Nor could he produce evidence of their conviction or of their having encroached upon public land. Upon appraisal of the evidence, the District Court decreed the suit and awarded general damages of Rs. 0.5 million.

12. Section 2(e) of the Defamation Ordinance defines publication to mean “the communication of the words to at least one person other than the person defamed and includes a newspaper or broadcast through the internet or other media.” An application to the police and/or the district administration constitutes communication of words to at least one person and, therefore, amounts to publication as correctly held by the learned District Court. Section 3 of the Defamation Ordinance provides that defamation constitutes “publication or circulation of a false statement or representation made orally or in written or visual form which injures the reputation of a person, tends to lower him in the estimation of others or tends to reduce him to ridicule, unjust criticism, dislike, contempt or hatred…” Written statements of a defamatory nature qualify as libel in terms of Section 3(2)(ii) of the Defamation Ordinance. Section 4 of the Defamation Ordinance provides that “the publication of defamatory matter is an actionable wrong without proof of special damage to the person defamed and where defamation is proved, damage shall be presumed.” In the case before us, the District Court found that the words admittedly used by the appellant were defamatory per se and therefore constituted an actionable wrong without proof of special damages.

13. The appellant’s defence while acknowledging his assertion that the respondents were part of “Qabza Mafia” and were seeking to encroach upon a graveyard and were liable for other illegal actions was that of truth. Section 5 of the Defamation Ordinance lists the defences that may be raised in defamation proceedings. Section 5(c) recognizes the truth of defamatory statements made for the public good as a valid defence. Further, Section 5(h) provides for absolute or qualified privilege as a defence in defamation proceedings. Section 6 defines absolute privilege, which is not relevant for present purposes. Section 7 provides for qualified privilege and states that “any fair and accurate publication of parliamentary proceedings or judicial proceedings which the public may attend and statements made to the proper authorities in order to procure the redress of public grievances shall have the protection of qualified privilege”. Although the appellant raised truth as a defence in the written statement filed before the District Court, we will also consider the question of qualified privilege, as it was considered by the District Court as well.

14. In terms of consequences and remedies, Section 9 provides that, where defamation stands proved, “the court may pass order directing the defendant to tender an apology, if acceptable to the plaintiff, and publish the same in similar manner and with the same prominence as the defamatory statements made and pay reasonable compensatory damages as general damages with a minimum of Rs.50,000 and in addition thereto, any special damage incurred that is proved by the plaintiff to the satisfaction of the court: provided that in case of the originator the minimum compensatory damages as general damages shall be three hundred thousand rupees.”

15. The appellant’s first argument that the falsity of the assertions made by him had not been proved is without merit. Calling an individual a member of a “Qabza Mafia” accuses that individual of organized land grabbing, which constitutes criminal conduct under the Pakistan Penal Code, 1860, as well as the Illegal Disposition Act, 2005. Calling the members of a family the Qabza Mafia and accusing them of usurping and encroaching upon land comprising a graveyard is not a statement of opinion. It is an imputation of organized criminality, extortion and moral turpitude. Such allegations fall within Sections 3 and 4 of the Defamation Ordinance and the traditional common-law principles applied in Pakistan. Where written words directly impute to a person the commission of a criminal offence, dishonest conduct or moral delinquency, the words are defamatory per se, as correctly held by the District Court. In such a case, there is no requirement for the plaintiff to plead or prove innuendo. The natural consequence of such an allegation is that an ordinary, reasonable reader or official would regard the person accused with suspicion and aversion and hold that person in lower estimation.

16. Once the plaintiff proves publication of words that are defamatory and refer to the plaintiff, it is for the defendant to prove truth as a defence in terms of Section 5(c) of the Defamation Ordinance. A defamatory statement is presumed to be false, malicious, and damaging, and the onus is therefore on the author of such a statement to prove its truth. In Khalid Aziz v. Pakistan Television (FAO No. 91-B/2006), decided by judgment dated 05.05.2017, this Court held that “in defamation cases, falsehood is presumed on the part of defendant, unless proved that the published or broadcasted materials were true. The plaintiff can only be burdened to prove the malice in case the defendant succeeds in proving that the defamatory words were true and privileged. Otherwise the court shall presume that the defamatory materials Published or broadcast Are false and mala fide exists on part of the defendant.”

17. It was held by the Sindh High Court in Syed Mehmood Ali v. Network Television Marketing Pvt. Ltd. (PLD 2005 Karachi 399) that “the initial burden of proving that the defamatory material was directed at the plaintiff rested upon the plaintiff. However, once the plaintiff successfully demonstrated that the damaging defamatory material was directed at him, the burden of establishing that the material was true or was not aimed at the plaintiff shifted to the defendant.” It was further held by the Sindh High Court in Mst. Bibi Saira and others v. P.O. Sindh through Secretary, Home Department, Govt. of Sindh and another (Civil Appeal No. S-26 of 2021), decided by judgment dated 22.04.2024, that “Once defamation is substantiated, the law invariably Infers detriment, injury, and diminution to the reputation, goodwill, or standing of an individual, their profession, or products, as applicable.” This principle is also reflected in Zafar Hijazi and others v. Muhammad Ayaz Mashwani (RFA No. 109-A of 2010), decided on 02.12.2019, wherein it was held that “In a suit for defamation, the defamatory words…are presumed in law to be false. The only burden on the plaintiff is to prove that the defamatory words were published by the defendants, whereafter the burden shifts to the defendants to prove that the words so published were true.” The Court further held that an action for defamation is actionable per se and that damage to the plaintiff’s reputation is presumed rather than required to be proved. The burden then shifts to the defendant to establish that the reporting or comments were based on true facts, were protected by privilege, concerned a matter of public interest, and did not tend to lower the plaintiff in the estimation of right-thinking members of society.

18. Under Section 5 of the Defamation Ordinance, truth is an affirmative defence. In terms of Articles 117, 119 and 122 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984, the burden of proving truth lies squarely on the party asserting it. It is a matter of common sense that a person cannot be required to prove a negative i.e. that he is not a land grabber. In the instant case, both the police and the district administration investigated the appellant’s complaints and found them to be without merit or evidentiary basis. The appellant’s failure to substantiate his plea of justification left the defamatory statements legally unexcused. Although the appellant raised truth as a defence and did not claim that his statements enjoyed qualified privilege, such privilege does not protect reckless and unverified slurs. The use of grossly disproportionate and vituperative language, branding five members of a family as the criminal Qabza Mafia, demonstrated recklessness and malice on the appellant’s part. A statement made to the proper authorities to procure redress of a public grievance would not be protected where it is found to have been actuated by malice or reckless disregard for the truth. The seminal case in this regard was Horrocks v Lowe [1975] AC 135, wherein it was held that “the plea of express malice destroys qualified privilege”. Malice in the context means that the defendant knows the allegation to be false, or that the defendant is recklessly indifferent to whether it is true or that the defendant dominant motive is improper such as spite or advantage in a private dispute. Although the defence of qualified privilege was not raised, the District Court took into account the fact that the appellant used a sweeping and inflammatory label to characterize all the respondents, who were members of the same family, and repeated the allegation in a second complaint after the first complaint had been filed, instead of making a factual report of a specific allegation in temperate language for investigation by the police or local administration. The District Court also took into account that the appellant was working as a stenographer in the district courts and was reasonably aware of the rights and entitlements of parties. Nevertheless, he continued to allege that the respondents were land grabbers and were involved in criminal conduct, allegations which were found to be untrue. In these circumstances, the District Court rightly concluded that the appellant’s words and conduct demonstrated recklessness and that malice could be presumed from his actions.

19. On the question of damages, as discussed above, where publication is in written form (libel) and is defamatory per se, damage is presumed by law. Section 9 of the Defamation Ordinance, reproduced above, provides for minimum compensatory damages of Rs. 300,000 in the case of an originator. In the instant case, the appellant was the originator, and the total compensation awarded to all the respondents was Rs. 500,000, which amounts to approximately Rs. 83,333 per respondent and falls within the threshold prescribed by Section 9. Although the Defamation Ordinance distinguishes between general damages and special damages, general damages constitute non-pecuniary compensation for loss of reputation, mental agony and distress caused to a person. Special damages, on the other hand, are quantifiable pecuniary losses caused by defamation, such as loss of employment or cancellation of a contract, which must be specifically pleaded and proved by the claimant. In the instant case, the District Court awarded only general damages, while taking into account the appellant’s financial capacity and the circumstances of the case. It is a settled principle that, in Pakistan, where the court determines and awards general damages, the measure for quantifying such damages is the rule of thumb, as they need not be proved. The appellant’s argument that the respondents had neither quantified nor proved their damages might have been relevant had the District Court awarded special damages, which it did not.

20. The right to freedom of speech is a fundamental right guaranteed by Article 19 of the Constitution of Pakistan, which is, however, subject to reasonable restrictions imposed by law. The Defamation Ordinance is one such law that imposes restrictions on freedom of speech in cases involving defamatory statements. It must also be remembered that Article 14 of the Constitution guarantees the dignity of citizens. Further, Article 4(2)(a) provides that “no action detrimental to life, liberty, body, reputation or property of any person shall be taken except in accordance with law.” While an individual’s right to freedom of speech must be protected, it must be balanced against the rights to dignity and reputation of those affected by such speech. It is for this purpose that Section 5 of the Defamation Ordinance provides appropriate defences. In the instant case, the respondents successfully established that the appellant had published words that were defamatory per se, on the basis of which the damage caused to the respondents was presumed. It was for the appellant to establish the defence of truth or privilege, which he failed to do, as correctly held by the District Court. Even in relation to damages, the approach of the District Court was fairly conservative and lenient, and does not warrant interference by this Court in its appellate jurisdiction.
21. In view of the above, this Court finds that the appeal is without merit and is dismissed with costs. Announced 22.10.2025 J U D G E (Approved for reporting)
(Abdul Saeed) SB Hon’ble Mr. Justice Babar Sattar, J
